label: def:slice-and-bilinear
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:slice-and-bilinear}
  Let $C\in B(H_1\otimes H_2)$ be given.
  \begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\arabic*)}]
  \par\hangindent 40\p@
    The \emph{bilinear form} of $C$ is the map
    $m_C(\tau,\tau')=\operatorname{Tr}\bigl((\tau\otimes\tau')C\bigr)$ on $\mathcal{T}(H_1)\times\mathcal{T}(H_2)$.
  \par\hangindent 40\p@
    The \emph{slice maps} of $C$ are the operators
    $T_C\colon\mathcal{T}(H_1)\to B(H_2)$ and $S_C\colon\mathcal{T}(H_2)\to B(H_1)$ determined by
    \[
      \operatorname{Tr}\bigl(\tau'\,T_C(\tau)\bigr)=m_C(\tau,\tau')=\operatorname{Tr}\bigl(\tau\,S_C(\tau')\bigr).
    \]
  \end{enumerate}
head: environment
name: Bilinear form and slice maps

label: lem:density
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For the first statement, suppose that a state $\omega$ is not in the weak$^*$ closure of the convex set $\mathfrak{D}(H)$.
  By the Hahn--Banach theorem, there is a self-adjoint $A\in B(H)$ with $\omega(A)>\sup_{\rho\in\mathfrak{D}(H)}\operatorname{Tr}(\rho A)=\sup\operatorname{spec}A$, which is impossible for a state.
  The second statement is the Jordan decomposition of the hermitian parts of $\omega$ (see~\cite[Section~4.3]{Kadison-Ringrose:1983b}).
head: environment

label: def:products
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:products}
  For states $\omega_1$ of $B(H_1)$ and $\omega_2$ of $B(H_2)$, and for $C\in B(H_1\otimes H_2)$, we define
  \[
    (\omega_1\otimes_{\mathsf{A}}\omega_2)(C)=\omega_2\bigl(Z_{\omega_1}\bigr),
    \qquad
    (\omega_1\otimes_{\mathsf{B}}\omega_2)(C)=\omega_1\bigl(W_{\omega_2}\bigr).
  \]
  The subscript names the system that is idealized first.
head: environment
name: The two products

label: lem:products
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:products}
  Let $(\rho_i)$ and $(\sigma_j)$ be nets of normal states with weak$^*$ limits $\omega_1$ and $\omega_2$, and let $C\in B(H_1\otimes H_2)$ be given.
  Then we have
  \[
    (\omega_1\otimes_{\mathsf{A}}\omega_2)(C)=\lim_j\lim_i\varphi_C(\rho_i,\sigma_j),
    \qquad
    (\omega_1\otimes_{\mathsf{B}}\omega_2)(C)=\lim_i\lim_j\varphi_C(\rho_i,\sigma_j).
  \]
  Moreover, with $T_C^{**}\colon B(H_1)^*\to B(H_2)^{**}$ the bitranspose of $T_C$, we have
  \[
    (\omega_1\otimes_{\mathsf{B}}\omega_2)(C)=\langle T_C^{**}(\omega_1),\omega_2\rangle,
    \qquad
    (\omega_1\otimes_{\mathsf{A}}\omega_2)(C)=\langle S_C^{**}(\omega_2),\omega_1\rangle .
  \]
  In particular, the map $\omega_2\mapsto(\omega_1\otimes_{\mathsf{A}}\omega_2)(C)$ is weak$^*$ continuous for every $C$, being evaluation at the operator $Z_{\omega_1}\in B(H_2)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For a normal state $\sigma$, we have
  \[
    \operatorname{Tr}(\sigma Z_{\omega_1})=\omega_1(S_C\sigma)
    =\lim_i\operatorname{Tr}(\rho_iS_C\sigma)=\lim_i\varphi_C(\rho_i,\sigma),
  \]
  and then $\omega_2(Z_{\omega_1})=\lim_j\operatorname{Tr}(\sigma_jZ_{\omega_1})$.
  The formula for $\otimes_{\mathsf{B}}$ is symmetric.
  Finally, we have $\langle T_C^{**}\omega_1,\omega_2\rangle=\omega_1(T_C^*\omega_2)=\omega_1(W_{\omega_2})$, and symmetrically for $S_C^{**}$.
head: environment

label: cor:normal-factor
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:normal-factor}
  If $\omega_1$ or $\omega_2$ is normal, then $(\omega_1\otimes_{\mathsf{A}}\omega_2)(C)=(\omega_1\otimes_{\mathsf{B}}\omega_2)(C)$ for every $C\in B(H_1\otimes H_2)$.
head: environment
name: Instability requires two idealized factors

title: Proof
body_md:
If $\omega_1$ is given by a density operator $\rho$, then we have $Z_{\omega_1}=T_C(\rho)$ and $(\omega_1\otimes_{\mathsf{B}}\omega_2)(C)=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho\,T_C^*\omega_2)=\omega_2(T_C\rho)$, so both products equal $\omega_2(T_C\rho)$.
  If $\omega_2$ is given by a density operator $\sigma$, then we have $T_C^*(\sigma)=S_C(\sigma)$, and both products equal $\omega_1(S_C\sigma)$.

label: def:stable
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:stable}
  Let $X$ and $Y$ be sets.
  A bounded function $f\colon X\times Y\to\mathbb{C}$ is \emph{stable} if for all sequences $(x_k)$ in $X$ and $(y_l)$ in $Y$, we have
  \[
    \lim_{l\to\infty}\lim_{k\to\infty}f(x_k,y_l)=\lim_{k\to\infty}\lim_{l\to\infty}f(x_k,y_l)
  \]
  whenever both iterated limits exist.
  An observable $C\in B(H_1\otimes H_2)$ is \emph{stable} if its expectation $\varphi_C(\rho,\sigma)=\operatorname{Tr}\bigl((\rho\otimes\sigma)C\bigr)$ is stable on $\mathfrak{D}(H_1)\times\mathfrak{D}(H_2)$.
head: environment
name: Double limit property

label: lem:ladder
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:ladder}
  Let $(a_{kl})_{k,l\in\mathbb{N}}$ be a bounded complex array, let $\mathcal{U}$ and $\mathcal{V}$ be nonprincipal ultrafilters on $\mathbb{N}$, and let
  \[
    L_1=\lim_{k,\mathcal{U}}\lim_{l,\mathcal{V}}a_{kl},\qquad L_2=\lim_{l,\mathcal{V}}\lim_{k,\mathcal{U}}a_{kl}
  \]
  be the two iterated limits.
  For every $\varepsilon>0$ there are indices $k_1<k_2<\cdots$ and $l_1<l_2<\cdots$ such that $|a_{k_il_m}-L_1|\le\varepsilon$ for $i\le m$ and $|a_{k_il_m}-L_2|\le\varepsilon$ for $i>m$.
head: environment
name: Ladder extraction

title: Proof
head: environment

label: cor:ultra-stable
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:ultra-stable}
  Let $X$ and $Y$ be sets, and let $f\colon X\times Y\to\mathbb{C}$ be a bounded function.
  Then the function $f$ is stable if and only if, for all sequences $(x_k)$ in $X$ and $(y_l)$ in $Y$ and all nonprincipal ultrafilters $\mathcal{U}$ and $\mathcal{V}$ on $\mathbb{N}$, we have
  \[
    \lim_{k,\mathcal{U}}\lim_{l,\mathcal{V}}f(x_k,y_l)=\lim_{l,\mathcal{V}}\lim_{k,\mathcal{U}}f(x_k,y_l).
  \]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
If ordinary iterated limits exist, they equal the ultrafilter ones;
  this gives one direction.
  For the other, suppose that the ultrafilter iterated limits are $L_1\neq L_2$.
  Apply \cref{lem:ladder} to $a_{kl}=f(x_k,y_l)$ with $2\varepsilon<|L_1-L_2|$, and pass to further subsequences $(k_{i_p})$ and $(l_{m_q})$ along which both ordinary iterated limits exist.
  For fixed $p$, we have $i_p\le m_q$ for all large $q$, so the limit over $q$ is within $\varepsilon$ of $L_1$, and hence so is the iterated limit $\lim_p\lim_q$.
  Symmetrically, the iterated limit $\lim_q\lim_p$ is within $\varepsilon$ of $L_2$.
  The two iterated limits differ, so the function $f$ is unstable.
head: environment

label: lem:preservation
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:preservation}
  Let $X$ and $Y$ be sets.
  \begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\alph*)}]
  \par\hangindent 40\p@
    \textup{(Sums with one-variable coefficients.)} Suppose that $f_1,\dots,f_r$ are stable on $X\times Y$ and $c_1,\dots,c_r\colon X\to\mathbb{C}$ and $d_1,\dots,d_r\colon Y\to\mathbb{C}$ are bounded.
    Then the function $\sum_jc_j(x)d_j(y)f_j(x,y)$ is stable.
    In particular, linear combinations of stable functions and separated sums $\sum_jc_j(x)d_j(y)$ are stable.
  \par\hangindent 40\p@
    \textup{(Uniform limits.)} If $f$ and $f'$ are bounded functions on $X\times Y$, the function $f'$ is stable and $\sup_{X\times Y}|f-f'|\le\varepsilon$, then any two iterated limits of $f$ differ by at most $2\varepsilon$.
    In particular, uniform limits of stable functions are stable.
  \par\hangindent 40\p@
    \textup{(Composition.)} If $f$ is stable on $X\times Y$ and $g\colon X'\to X$ and $h\colon Y'\to Y$ are maps, then the function $(x',y')\mapsto f(g(x'),h(y'))$ is stable on $X'\times Y'$.
  \par\hangindent 40\p@
    \textup{(Reduction to states.)} For $C\in B(H_1\otimes H_2)$, the expectation $\varphi_C$ is stable on $\mathfrak{D}(H_1)\times\mathfrak{D}(H_2)$ if and only if the bilinear form $m_C$ is stable on the product of the unit balls of $\mathcal{T}(H_1)$ and $\mathcal{T}(H_2)$.
  \end{enumerate}
head: environment
name: Preservation of stability

title: Proof
body_md:
(a) Put $F=\sum_jc_jd_jf_j$, and let $(x_k)$ and $(y_l)$ be sequences along which both iterated limits of $F$ exist.
  Pass to subsequences along which every $c_j(x_k)$ and every $d_j(y_l)$ converges, say to $c_j^*$ and $d_j^*$, and both iterated limits of every $f_j$ exist.
  By stability, the two iterated limits of $f_j$ agree, say with $\Lambda_j$, and both iterated limits of $F$ along the subsequences equal $\sum_jc_j^*d_j^*\Lambda_j$.

  (b) Let $L_1$ and $L_2$ be iterated limits of $f$.
  Pass to subsequences along which both iterated limits of $f'$ exist.
  They are equal, say to $\Lambda$, and we have $|L_1-\Lambda|\le\varepsilon$ and $|L_2-\Lambda|\le\varepsilon$.

  (c) Sequences in $X'$ and $Y'$ are mapped to sequences in $X$ and $Y$.

  (d) One direction is trivial.
  For the other, decompose each $\tau$ in the unit ball of
  $\mathcal{T}(H)$ as $\tau=c_1\rho_1-c_2\rho_2+ic_3\rho_3-ic_4\rho_4$, using the positive and negative parts of the hermitian parts of $\tau$, with $\rho_j\in\mathfrak{D}(H)$ and $0\le c_j\le1$ (choosing a fixed state when a part vanishes).
  These choices define maps $\tau\mapsto\rho_j(\tau)$ and bounded coefficients $\tau\mapsto c_j(\tau)$.
  The value $m_C(\tau,\tau')$ is then a sum of sixteen terms of the form $\pm c_j(\tau)c'_{j'}(\tau') \varphi_C(\rho_j(\tau),\rho'_{j'}(\tau'))$, with factors $\pm1$ or $\pm i$, so parts (a) and (c) apply.

title: Theorem

title: Proof
body_md:
For $C'=\sum_jA_j\otimes B_j$, we have $\varphi_{C'}(\rho,\sigma)=\sum_j\operatorname{Tr}(\rho A_j)\operatorname{Tr}(\sigma B_j)$, which is stable by \cref{lem:preservation}(a), and $|\varphi_C-\varphi_{C'}|\le\|C-C'\|$.

label: cor:compact-and-findim
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:compact-and-findim}
  \leavevmode
  \begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\alph*)}]
  \par\hangindent 40\p@
    Every compact operator on $H_1\otimes H_2$, in particular every finite-rank projection such as a Bell-state projection, is stable.
  \par\hangindent 40\p@
    If $H_1$ or $H_2$ is finite-dimensional, then every $C\in B(H_1\otimes H_2)$ is stable.
  \end{enumerate}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
(a) The rank-one operators $|\psi\otimes\chi\rangle\langle\psi'\otimes\chi'|=|\psi\rangle\langle\psi'|\otimes|\chi\rangle\langle\chi'|$ span a dense subspace of the compact operators.
  (b) If $H_1$ has dimension $n$, then $C=\sum_{i,j\le n}|e_i\rangle\langle e_j|\otimes C_{ij}$ for suitable $C_{ij}\in B(H_2)$, so the operator $C$ lies in $B(H_1)\odot B(H_2)$.

label: prop:notmin
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:notmin}
  If $C\in B(H_1)\otimes_{\min}B(H_2)$, then the slice map $T_C$ is compact.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The slice map $T_{A\otimes B}=\operatorname{Tr}(\,\cdot\,A)B$ has rank one, and $\|T_C-T_{C'}\|\le\|C-C'\|$;
  norm limits of finite-rank operators are compact.

label: prop:hilbertfactor
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:hilbertfactor}
  Let $X$ and $Y$ be sets, let $\mathcal{H}$ be a Hilbert space, and let $u\colon X\to\mathcal{H}$ and $v\colon Y\to\mathcal{H}$ be bounded maps.
  Then the function $f(x,y)=\langle u(x),v(y)\rangle$ is stable.
  In particular, if $\varphi_C(\rho,\sigma)=\langle u(\rho),v(\sigma)\rangle$ for bounded maps $u\colon\mathfrak{D}(H_1)\to\mathcal{H}$ and $v\colon\mathfrak{D}(H_2)\to\mathcal{H}$, then the observable $C$ is stable.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Bounded sets in a Hilbert space are relatively weakly sequentially compact.
  Given sequences $(x_k)$ and $(y_l)$ along which both iterated limits exist, pass to subsequences with $u(x_{k_i})\rightharpoonup\xi$ and $v(y_{l_j})\rightharpoonup\xi'$.
  For each $i$, we have $\lim_j\langle u(x_{k_i}),v(y_{l_j})\rangle=\langle u(x_{k_i}),\xi'\rangle$, which tends to $\langle\xi,\xi'\rangle$;
  the other iterated limit is also $\langle\xi,\xi'\rangle$.
head: environment

label: lem:swaptrick
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:swaptrick}
  For all $\tau_1,\tau_2\in\mathcal{T}(K)$, we have $\operatorname{Tr}\bigl((\tau_1\otimes\tau_2)F\bigr)=\operatorname{Tr}(\tau_1\tau_2)$.
head: environment
name: Swap trick

title: Proof
body_md:
For $\tau_1=|\psi\rangle\langle\psi'|$ and $\tau_2=|\chi\rangle\langle\chi'|$, one computes $(\tau_1\otimes\tau_2)F=|\psi\otimes\chi\rangle\langle\chi'\otimes\psi'|$, whose trace is $\langle\psi,\chi'\rangle\langle\chi,\psi'\rangle=\operatorname{Tr}(\tau_1\tau_2)$.
  Extend by bilinearity and continuity.
head: environment

label: prop:comparison
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:comparison}
  Let $A$ and $B$ be as above.
  \begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\arabic*)}]
  \par\hangindent 40\p@
    The projection $[A=B]$ is stable.
    If $A$ and $B$ have infinitely many common eigenvalues, then the projection $[A=B]$ does not belong to $B(H_1)\otimes_{\min}B(H_2)$.
  \par\hangindent 40\p@
    If $A$ or $B$ has finitely many eigenvalues, then the projection $[A<B]$ is stable.
  \par\hangindent 40\p@
    If the point spectra of $A$ and $B$ are both unbounded above, then the projection $[A<B]$ is unstable.
  \end{enumerate}
head: environment
name: Equality is stable, order is not

title: Proof
body_md:
(1) We have $\varphi_{[A=B]}(\rho,\sigma)=\sum_\lambda\operatorname{Tr}(\rho \Pi^A_\lambda)\operatorname{Tr}(\sigma \Pi^B_\lambda) =\langle u(\rho),v(\sigma)\rangle_{\ell^2}$, where
  $u(\rho)=(\operatorname{Tr}\rho\Pi^A_\lambda)_\lambda$ and $v(\sigma)=(\operatorname{Tr}\sigma\Pi^B_\lambda)_\lambda$ are vectors of $\ell^2$-norm at most one, so \cref{prop:hilbertfactor} applies.
  For each common eigenvalue $\lambda$, pick a unit vector $\psi_\lambda$ in the range of $\Pi^A_\lambda$.
  Then $T_{[A=B]}(\psi_\lambda)=\Pi^B_\lambda$, and these are mutually orthogonal nonzero projections, so the slice map $T_{[A=B]}$ is not compact;
  apply \cref{prop:notmin}.

  (2) If $A$ has finitely many eigenvalues, then $[A<B]=\sum_{\lambda} \Pi^A_{\lambda}\otimes\bigl(\sum_{\lambda'>\lambda}\Pi^B_{\lambda'}\bigr)$ is a finite sum of products, and \cref{thm:stable} applies.
  If $B$ has finitely many eigenvalues, the same argument applies to $[A<B]=\sum_{\lambda'}\bigl(\sum_{\lambda<\lambda'}\Pi^A_{\lambda}\bigr)\otimes\Pi^B_{\lambda'}$.

  (3) Choose eigenvalues $\lambda_1<\lambda'_1<\lambda_2<\lambda'_2<\cdots$, with $\lambda_k$ an eigenvalue of $A$ with unit eigenvector $\psi_k$ and $\lambda'_l$ an eigenvalue of $B$ with unit eigenvector $\chi_l$.
  Then $\varphi_{[A<B]}(\psi_k,\chi_l)$ is $1$ if $k\le l$ and $0$ if $k>l$, so the two iterated limits are $0$ and $1$.

label: thm:unstable
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:unstable}
  Let $(e_k)$ and $(f_l)$ be orthonormal sequences in $H_1$ and $H_2$, and let $P_{k<l}$ be the projection onto the closed span of $\{e_k\otimes f_l:k<l\}$.
  Then $\varphi_{P_{k<l}}(e_k,f_l)$ is $1$ if $k<l$ and $0$ otherwise, so
  \[
    \lim_{l}\lim_{k}\varphi_{P_{k<l}}(e_k,f_l)=0\neq1=\lim_{k}\lim_{l}\varphi_{P_{k<l}}(e_k,f_l).
  \]
  Hence the projection $P_{k<l}$ is unstable, and its distance to $B(H_1)\otimes_{\min}B(H_2)$ is at least $\tfrac12$.
head: environment
name: Instability of the order projection

title: Proof
body_md:
The values form the staircase
  \[
    \begin{pmatrix}
             & f_1    & f_2    & f_3    & \cdots \\
      e_1    & 0      & 1      & 1      & \cdots \\
      e_2    & 0      & 0      & 1      & \cdots \\
      e_3    & 0      & 0      & 0      & \cdots \\
      \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \ddots
    \end{pmatrix}
  \]
  Each column tends to $0$ and each row to $1$.
  The bound on the distance follows from \cref{thm:stable}.

label: thm:weakcompact
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:weakcompact}
  For every $C\in B(H_1\otimes H_2)$, the following are equivalent:
  \begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\arabic*)}]
  \par\hangindent 40\p@
    The observable $C$ is stable.
  \par\hangindent 40\p@
    The bilinear form $m_C$ is stable on the product of the unit balls of $\mathcal{T}(H_1)$ and $\mathcal{T}(H_2)$.
  \par\hangindent 40\p@
    \textup{(Topology.)} The slice map $T_C\colon\mathcal{T}(H_1)\to B(H_2)$ is weakly compact.
  \par\hangindent 40\p@
    \textup{(Geometry.)} There are a reflexive Banach space $E$ and bounded operators $a\colon\mathcal{T}(H_1)\to E$ and $J\colon E\to B(H_2)$ with $T_C=J\circ a$.
  \par\hangindent 40\p@
    \textup{(Algebra.)} For all states $\omega_1$ of $B(H_1)$ and $\omega_2$ of $B(H_2)$, we have $(\omega_1\otimes_{\mathsf{A}}\omega_2)(C)=(\omega_1\otimes_{\mathsf{B}}\omega_2)(C)$.
    Equivalently, for every state $\omega_1$ of $B(H_1)$, we have $T_C^{**}(\omega_1)\in B(H_2)$, and then $T_C^{**}(\omega_1)=Z_{\omega_1}$.
  \par\hangindent 40\p@[\textup{(5$'$)}]
    The equality in \textup{(5)} holds for all ultralimit states $\omega_1=\lim_{k,\mathcal{U}}\rho_k$ and $\omega_2=\lim_{l,\mathcal{V}}\sigma_l$ of sequences of normal states.
  \par\hangindent 40\p@
    \textup{(Separate continuity.)} There is a function $\hat\varphi\colon\mathcal{S}(B(H_1))\times\mathcal{S}(B(H_2))\to\mathbb{C}$, weak$^*$ continuous in each variable separately, with $\hat\varphi(\rho,\sigma)=\varphi_C(\rho,\sigma)$ for all normal states $\rho$ and $\sigma$.
  \end{enumerate}
head: environment
name: Characterization of stability

title: Proof
head: environment
name: Proof of the first step

title: Proof
body_md:
We show that \textup{(3)} and \textup{(4)} are equivalent.
  If $T_C$ is weakly compact, it factors through a reflexive space by the Davis--Figiel--Johnson--Pełczyński theorem, and then we have
  $\varphi_C(\rho,\sigma)=\operatorname{Tr}(\sigma\,J(a\rho))=\langle a(\rho),J^*(\sigma)\rangle$, which is the commutativity of~\eqref{eq:thm-reflexive}.
  Conversely, the image under $a$ of the unit ball is bounded, hence relatively weakly compact in the reflexive space $E$, and $J$ is weak-to-weak continuous.
head: environment
name: Proof of the second step

title: Proof
body_md:
We show that (3) and (5) are equivalent, that (5) implies (5$'$), which implies (1), and that (5) and (6) are equivalent;
  together with the first two steps, this proves the theorem.
  We first show that (3) and (5) are equivalent.
  For a state $\omega_1$ and a normal state $\sigma$, we have $\langle T_C^{**}\omega_1,\sigma\rangle=\omega_1(T_C^*\sigma)=\omega_1(S_C\sigma) =\operatorname{Tr}(\sigma Z_{\omega_1})$.
  Hence the functional $T_C^{**}(\omega_1)$ belongs to $B(H_2)$ if and only if
  $T_C^{**}(\omega_1)=Z_{\omega_1}$, and by \cref{lem:products}, this happens if and only if $(\omega_1\otimes_{\mathsf{B}}\omega_2)(C)=\omega_2(Z_{\omega_1})=(\omega_1\otimes_{\mathsf{A}}\omega_2)(C)$ for all states $\omega_2$.
  Since states span $B(H_1)^*$ (see \cref{lem:density}), condition~(5) says that $T_C^{**}(B(H_1)^*)\subseteq B(H_2)$, which is~(3) by Gantmacher’s theorem.

  The implication from (5) to (5$'$) is trivial.
  For the implication from (5$'$) to (1), suppose that $C$ is unstable.
  There are sequences whose ordinary iterated limits differ, and by \cref{lem:products}, the ultralimit states along any nonprincipal $\mathcal{U}$ and $\mathcal{V}$ reproduce these limits as the two products.

  Finally, we show that (5) and (6) are equivalent.
  By \cref{lem:products}, the maps $\omega_2\mapsto(\omega_1\otimes_{\mathsf{A}}\omega_2)(C)=\omega_2(Z_{\omega_1})$ and $\omega_1\mapsto(\omega_1\otimes_{\mathsf{B}}\omega_2)(C)=\omega_1(W_{\omega_2})$ are weak$^*$ continuous, so under~(5) their common value is separately continuous.
  Conversely, let $\hat\varphi$ be as in~(6).
  For a normal state $\sigma$ and a net $(\rho_i)$ of normal states with limit $\omega_1$, continuity in the first variable gives $\hat\varphi(\omega_1,\sigma)=\lim_i\varphi_C(\rho_i,\sigma)=(\omega_1\otimes_{\mathsf{A}}\sigma)(C)$.
  Both $\hat\varphi(\omega_1,\cdot\,)$ and $(\omega_1\otimes_{\mathsf{A}}\cdot\,)(C)$ are weak$^*$ continuous and normal states are dense, so we have $\hat\varphi=\otimes_{\mathsf{A}}$.
  Symmetrically, we have $\hat\varphi=\otimes_{\mathsf{B}}$, which is~(5).
head: environment
name: Proof of the third step

label: prop:pure
title: Proposition
head: environment
name: Pure probes suffice

title: Proof
body_md:
The idea is to represent effective observables as continuous functions on the closure of the pure states of $B(H_2)$, where Grothendieck’s criterion needs to test only a dense set of points.
  For density operators we have $\varphi_{C^*}=\overline{\varphi_C}$, so the hermitian parts of $C$ inherit the hypothesis, and we may assume that $C$ is self-adjoint;
  then the operator $T_C(\rho)$ is self-adjoint for $\rho\ge0$.
  Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathcal{S}(B(H_2))$ be the weak$^*$ closure of the pure states, a compact space.
  For a self-adjoint operator $A$, the function $\hat{A}(\omega)=\omega(A)$ on $\Omega$ satisfies $\sup_\Omega|\hat{A}|=\|A\|$, so the map $A\mapsto\hat{A}$ is a linear isometry of the self-adjoint part of $B(H_2)$ onto a closed subspace of $C(\Omega)$.
  Since the pure states are dense in $\Omega$, restriction to the set $\mathsf{P}_2$ of pure states of Bob’s system is a linear isometry of $C(\Omega)$ onto a closed subspace of the space $\ell^\infty(\mathsf{P}_2)$ of bounded functions on $\mathsf{P}_2$.
  By Grothendieck’s criterion for bounded subsets of
  $\ell^\infty$ of a set~\cite{Grothendieck:1952} (see also~\cite{Ptak:1963b}),
  the double limit property of the hypothesis shows that the restrictions of the functions
  $\omega\mapsto\omega(T_C\psi)$, for pure states $\psi$ of Alice’s system, form a relatively weakly compact subset of $\ell^\infty(\mathsf{P}_2)$, and hence the functions themselves form a relatively weakly compact subset of $C(\Omega)$.
  By the Hahn--Banach theorem, relative weak compactness passes to the closed subspace, so the set of operators $T_C\psi$, for $\psi$ pure, is relatively weakly compact.
  By Krein’s theorem, its closed convex hull is weakly compact.
  This hull contains $T_C(\mathfrak{D}(H_1))$, because every density operator is a trace-norm convergent convex combination of pure states.
  Arguing as at the end of the first step of the proof of \cref{thm:weakcompact}, the slice map $T_C$ is weakly compact.

label: thm:polyapprox
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:polyapprox}

head: environment
name: Affine simulation

title: Proof
body_md:
We first show that (1) implies (2) and (3).
  The idea is that, under stability, the idealized response is an actual operator in the weak closure of a convex set of actual responses, and Mazur’s theorem converts weak approximation into norm approximation.
  By \cref{thm:weakcompact}, we have $T_C^{**}(\omega_1)=Z_{\omega_1}\in B(H_2)$, and both products equal $\omega_2(Z_{\omega_1})$.
  If $\omega_1=\lim_{k,\mathcal{U}}\rho_k$, then the state $\omega_1$ lies in the weak$^*$ closure of the convex hull of $\{\rho_k:k\ge n\}$.
  The bitranspose $T_C^{**}$ is weak$^*$-to-weak$^*$ continuous, and on $B(H_2)$ the weak$^*$ topology of $B(H_2)^{**}$ is the weak topology.
  Hence the operator $Z_{\omega_1}$ lies in the weak closure of the convex set $T_C(\operatorname{conv}\{\rho_k:k\ge n\})$, hence in its norm closure by Mazur’s theorem:
  there is $\rho$ in that convex hull with $\|Z_{\omega_1}-T_C(\rho)\|\le\varepsilon$, and then $|\omega_2(Z_{\omega_1}-T_C\rho)|\le\varepsilon$ for every state $\omega_2$.
  The same argument applies to nets.

  \emph{Proof that (2) implies (1).}
  By \cref{lem:products}, the functional $G=T_C^{**}(\omega_1)-T_C(\rho)$ on $B(H_2)^*$ satisfies $|G(\omega_2)|\le\varepsilon$ for all states $\omega_2$, and hence we have $\|G\|\le4\varepsilon$ by \cref{lem:density}.
  Hence the functional $T_C^{**}(\omega_1)$ lies within $4\varepsilon$ of $B(H_2)$ for every $\varepsilon$, hence in $B(H_2)$, and this holds for every state $\omega_1$.
  By \cref{thm:weakcompact}(5), the observable $C$ is stable.

  \emph{Proof that (3) implies (1).}
  Let $(\rho_k)$ and $(\sigma_l)$ be sequences along which the ordinary iterated limits
  \[
    L_1=\lim_k\lim_l\varphi_C(\rho_k,\sigma_l),\qquad
    L_2=\lim_l\lim_k\varphi_C(\rho_k,\sigma_l)
  \]
  exist.
  Let $\mathcal{U}$ be a nonprincipal ultrafilter, let $\omega_1=\lim_{k,\mathcal{U}}\rho_k$ and $\omega_2=\lim_{l,\mathcal{U}}\sigma_l$, and put $\alpha_k=\lim_l\varphi_C(\rho_k,\sigma_l)=\omega_2(T_C\rho_k)$.
  Then we have $(\omega_1\otimes_{\mathsf{A}}\omega_2)(C)=L_2$.
  Given $\varepsilon>0$, choose $n$ with $|\alpha_k-L_1|\le\varepsilon$ for all $k\ge n$, and choose $\rho=\sum_{k\ge n}t_k\rho_k$ as in~(3).
  Then we have
  \[
    |L_2-L_1|\le|L_2-\omega_2(T_C\rho)|+\Bigl|\sum_kt_k\alpha_k-L_1\Bigr|\le2\varepsilon .
  \]

label: exa:order-matters
title: Example
body_md:
\label{exa:order-matters}
  Let $(e_k)_{k\ge0}$ and $(f_l)_{l\ge1}$ be orthonormal bases of $H_1$ and $H_2$, let $S_k$ be the projection onto the span of $f_1,\dots,f_k$, and put
  \[
    P=|e_0\rangle\langle e_0|\otimes I+\sum_{k\ge1}|e_k\rangle\langle e_k|\otimes S_k .
  \]
  The operator $P$ is a projection, and for $k\ge1$ we have $\varphi_P(e_k,f_l)=1$ if and only if $l\le k$, so the projection $P$ is unstable.
  On the other hand, the operator $T_P(\rho)$ is diagonal, with $l$-th diagonal entry $\rho_{00}+\sum_{k\ge l}\rho_{kk}$.
  These entries form a nonincreasing sequence in $[0,1]$ whose first term is $1$, and every such sequence $(c_l)$ arises, from $\rho_{kk}=c_k-c_{k+1}$ and $\rho_{00}=\lim_lc_l$.
  The set of these diagonal operators is weak$^*$ closed, so for every state $\omega_1$, the operator $Z_{\omega_1}$, which lies in the weak$^*$ closure of $T_P(\mathfrak{D}(H_1))$, equals $T_P(\rho)$ for some actual $\rho$.
  Thus $(\omega_1\otimes_{\mathsf{A}}\omega_2)(P)=\omega_2(T_P\rho)$ exactly, for all states $\omega_2$.
  For $\omega_1=\lim_{k,\mathcal{U}}e_k$, the simulating state is $e_0$;
  but for $\omega_2=\lim_{l,\mathcal{U}}f_l$, we have $(\omega_1\otimes_{\mathsf{B}}\omega_2)(P)=0\ne1$.

name: Monte Carlo simulation

title: Proof
body_md:
For $\xi\in\mathcal{H}$, let $B_\xi\in B(H_2)$ be the operator with $\operatorname{Tr}(\tau'B_\xi)=\langle\xi,b(\tau')\rangle$ for all $\tau'\in\mathcal{T}(H_2)$.
  The map $\xi\mapsto B_\xi$ is linear, we have $\|B_\xi\|\le\|b\|\,\|\xi\|$, and $T_C(\rho)=B_{a(\rho)}$.
  Let $\xi^*$ be the weak limit of $a(\rho_k)$ along $\mathcal{U}$.
  For a normal state $\sigma$, we have $\operatorname{Tr}(\sigma Z_{\omega_1})=\lim_{k,\mathcal{U}}\langle a(\rho_k),b(\sigma)\rangle=\langle\xi^*,b(\sigma)\rangle$, so we have $Z_{\omega_1}=B_{\xi^*}$.
  By Mazur’s theorem, there is a finite convex combination $\xi=\sum_{k\ge n}t_ka(\rho_k)$ with $\|\xi^*-\xi\|\le\varepsilon/(2\|b\|)$.
  Let $\kappa_1,\dots,\kappa_M$ be independent random indices with $\Pr[\kappa_j=k]=t_k$.
  Since the summands are independent with expectation $\xi$, we have
  \[
    \mathbb{E}\Bigl\|\xi-\frac1M\sum_{j=1}^Ma(\rho_{\kappa_j})\Bigr\|^2
    =\frac1M\,\mathbb{E}\bigl\|a(\rho_{\kappa_1})-\xi\bigr\|^2\le\frac{R_a^2}{M},
  \]
  so some realization $k_1,\dots,k_M$ satisfies $\|\xi-\frac1M\sum_ja(\rho_{k_j})\|\le R_a/\sqrt M\le\varepsilon/(2\|b\|)$.
  Hence $\|Z_{\omega_1}-T_C\bar\rho\|=\|B_{\xi^*-a(\bar\rho)}\|\le\varepsilon$.
  Stability follows from \cref{prop:hilbertfactor}.

title: Theorem

\label{thm:fubini}
  An observable $C\in B(H_1\otimes H_2)$ is stable if and only if for all means $\mu$ on $\mathfrak{D}(H_1)$ and $\nu$ on $\mathfrak{D}(H_2)$, we have
  \[
    \int\!\!\Bigl(\int\varphi_C(\rho,\sigma)\,d\mu(\rho)\Bigr)d\nu(\sigma)
    =\int\!\!\Bigl(\int\varphi_C(\rho,\sigma)\,d\nu(\sigma)\Bigr)d\mu(\rho).

head: environment
name: Fubini’s theorem for means

title: Proof
body_md:
The idea is that, since the expectation is affine in each state, iterated integrals depend only on barycenters, and so they are the two products of \cref{sec:setting}.
  Since $\varphi_C(\rho,\sigma)=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho\,S_C\sigma)$ is affine in $\rho$, we have $\int\varphi_C(\rho,\sigma)\,d\mu(\rho)=\omega_\mu(S_C\sigma) =\operatorname{Tr}(\sigma Z_{\omega_\mu})$, and integrating against $\nu$ gives $(\omega_\mu\otimes_{\mathsf{A}}\omega_\nu)(C)$.
  Symmetrically, the other iterated integral is $(\omega_\mu\otimes_{\mathsf{B}}\omega_\nu)(C)$.
  Every state $\omega$ is a barycenter:
  by \cref{lem:density}, there is a net $(\rho_i)$ of normal states with limit $\omega$, and if $\mathcal{W}$ is an ultrafilter on its index set containing all tails, then $\mu(g)=\lim_{i,\mathcal{W}}g(\rho_i)$ defines a mean with barycenter $\omega$.
  Thus the identity holds for all means if and only if condition~(5) of \cref{thm:weakcompact} holds, that is, if and only if $C$ is stable.

label: thm:independent-product
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:independent-product}
  For all states $\omega_1$ of $B(H_1)$ and $\omega_2$ of $B(H_2)$, the following hold:
  \begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\alph*)}]
  \par\hangindent 40\p@
    \textup{(Existence.)} The functional $\omega_1\otimes\omega_2$ is a state of $\mathcal{O}$:
    it is linear, positive on positive elements of $\mathcal{O}$, and takes the value $1$ at $I$.
  \par\hangindent 40\p@
    \textup{(Extension.)} If $\omega_1$ and $\omega_2$ are given by density operators $\rho$ and $\sigma$, then $(\omega_1\otimes\omega_2)(C)=\operatorname{Tr}((\rho\otimes\sigma)C)$ for all $C\in\mathcal{O}$.
  \par\hangindent 40\p@
    \textup{(Uniqueness.)} For every $C\in\mathcal{O}$, the assignment $(\omega_1,\omega_2)\mapsto (\omega_1\otimes\omega_2)(C)$ is separately weak$^*$ continuous, and it is the only separately weak$^*$ continuous function on $\mathcal{S}(B(H_1))\times\mathcal{S}(B(H_2))$ that satisfies~\textup{(b)}.
  \par\hangindent 40\p@
    \textup{(Symmetry.)} For every $C\in\mathcal{O}$, the observable $F_{12}CF_{12}^*$ on $H_2\otimes H_1$ is stable, and $(\omega_2\otimes\omega_1)(F_{12}CF_{12}^*)=(\omega_1\otimes\omega_2)(C)$.
  \end{enumerate}
  Moreover, an observable $C\in B(H_1\otimes H_2)$ is stable if and only if the two products $\otimes_{\mathsf{A}}$ and $\otimes_{\mathsf{B}}$ agree at $C$ for all pairs of states.
head: environment
name: The independent product

title: Proof
body_md:
(a) The slice map $S_C$ is linear in $C$, and so is $(\omega_1\otimes_{\mathsf{A}}\omega_2)(C)=\omega_2(S_C^*\omega_1)$.
  If $C\ge0$ and $\sigma\ge0$, then we have $S_C(\sigma)\ge0$, so $\operatorname{Tr}(\sigma Z_{\omega_1})=\omega_1(S_C\sigma)\ge0$ for every positive $\sigma$;
  hence $Z_{\omega_1}\ge0$ and $(\omega_1\otimes_{\mathsf{A}}\omega_2)(C)=\omega_2(Z_{\omega_1})\ge0$.
  For $C=I$, we have $S_I(\sigma)=\operatorname{Tr}(\sigma)I$ and $Z_{\omega_1}=I$.

  (b) This is \cref{cor:normal-factor}.

  (c) This is the proof that (5) and (6) are equivalent in \cref{thm:weakcompact}.

  (d) Write $C'=F_{12}CF_{12}^*$.
  For density operators we have $\varphi_{C'}(\sigma,\rho)=\varphi_C(\rho,\sigma)$, so the observable $C'$ is stable by \cref{lem:preservation}(c).
  Let $(\rho_i)$ and $(\sigma_j)$ be nets of normal states with limits $\omega_1$ and $\omega_2$.
  By \cref{lem:products}, the product $(\omega_2\otimes_{\mathsf{B}}\omega_1)(C')$, in which the second factor $\omega_1$ is idealized first, equals $\lim_j\lim_i\varphi_{C'}(\sigma_j,\rho_i)=\lim_j\lim_i\varphi_C(\rho_i,\sigma_j) =(\omega_1\otimes_{\mathsf{A}}\omega_2)(C)$.
  Both sides are the respective independent products.

  The final statement is the equivalence of~(1) and~(5) in \cref{thm:weakcompact}.

label: prop:ladders-to-trees
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:ladders-to-trees}
  Every $\delta$-ladder of length $2^{n+1}-1$ for $C$ yields a $\delta$-tree of height $n$ for $C$, with the same $\gamma$ and $\theta$ and with leaves and nodes taken from the ladder.
head: environment
name: Ladders give trees

title: Proof
body_md:
For $s$ of length at most $n$, put
  \[
    \operatorname{pos}(s)=\sum_{k<|s|}\bigl(1-s(k)\bigr)2^{-(k+1)}+2^{-(|s|+1)}\in(0,1).
  \]
  The binary expansion of $\operatorname{pos}(s)$ is $1-s(0),\dots,1-s(|s|-1),1$, so the map $\operatorname{pos}$ is injective, and its image has $2^{n+1}-1$ elements.
  We claim that if $s{}^\frown \iota\sqsubseteq\eta$ with $\eta\in2^n$, then we have $\operatorname{pos}(\eta)<\operatorname{pos}(s)$ if and only if $\iota=1$.
  Indeed, with $k=|s|$, we have
  \[
    \operatorname{pos}(\eta)-\operatorname{pos}(s)=-\iota\,2^{-(k+1)}+\varrho,\qquad
    \varrho=\sum_{k<j<n}\bigl(1-\eta(j)\bigr)2^{-(j+1)}+2^{-(n+1)},
  \]
  and $0<\varrho\le(2^{-(k+1)}-2^{-n})+2^{-(n+1)}<2^{-(k+1)}$.
  The bound $0<\varrho<2^{-(k+1)}$ is the point of the construction:
  the digits after position $k$ can move $\operatorname{pos}(\eta)$ by less than the digit at position $k$, so the turn taken at $s$ alone decides on which side of $\operatorname{pos}(s)$ the leaf lies.

  Let $\rho_1,\dots,\rho_N$ and $\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_N$, with $N=2^{n+1}-1$, be the states of the ladder, and let $\pi$ be the increasing bijection from the image of $\operatorname{pos}$ onto $\{1,\dots,N\}$.
  Put $\rho_\eta=\rho_{\pi(\operatorname{pos}(\eta))}$ for $\eta\in2^n$ and $\sigma_s=\sigma_{\pi(\operatorname{pos}(s))}$ for $s\in2^{<n}$.
  If $s{}^\frown \iota\sqsubseteq\eta$ and $\iota=1$, then $\pi(\operatorname{pos}(\eta))<\pi(\operatorname{pos}(s))$, and the ladder gives $\theta(\varphi_C(\rho_\eta,\sigma_s)-\gamma)\ge\delta/2$;
  if $\iota=0$, then $\pi(\operatorname{pos}(\eta))>\pi(\operatorname{pos}(s))$, and the ladder gives the opposite inequality.

body_md:
\label{thm:uniform}
  For every self-adjoint $C\in B(H_1\otimes H_2)$, the following are equivalent:
  \begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\arabic*)}]
  \par\hangindent 40\p@
    The observable $C$ is uniformly stable.
  \par\hangindent 40\p@
    For every $\delta>0$, the heights of $\delta$-trees for $C$ are bounded.
  \par\hangindent 40\p@
    The ultrapower expectation $\Phi^\mathcal{U}_C$ is stable for every nonprincipal ultrafilter $\mathcal{U}$.
  \par\hangindent 40\p@
    The ultrapower expectation $\Phi^\mathcal{U}_C$ is stable for some nonprincipal ultrafilter $\mathcal{U}$.
  \end{enumerate}
  If these conditions fail, then there is $\delta>0$ such that for every nonprincipal $\mathcal{U}$, there is an infinite $\delta$-tree for $\Phi^\mathcal{U}_C$.
  Every uniformly stable observable is stable.
head: environment
name: Uniform stability

title: Proof
body_md:
The implication from (2) to (1) is \cref{prop:ladders-to-trees}.

  \emph{Proof that (1) implies (3).}
  Suppose that $\Phi^\mathcal{U}_C$ is unstable.
  The proof of \cref{prop:inst-ladder} uses only \cref{lem:ladder}, which holds for any bounded function on a product of sets, so it gives an infinite $\delta$-ladder $(x_i,y_j)$ for $\Phi^\mathcal{U}_C$.
  Fix $N$.
  For each of the $N^2$ pairs $i,j\le N$, the set of $k$ with $\theta(\varphi_C(x_{i,k},y_{j,k})-\gamma)\ge\delta/4$ (if $i\le j$), respectively $\le-\delta/4$ (if $i>j$), belongs to $\mathcal{U}$.
  For $k$ in the intersection of these sets, the states $x_{i,k}$ and $y_{j,k}$ form a $\delta/2$-ladder of length $N$ for $C$.
  Hence the observable $C$ is not uniformly stable.

  The implication from (3) to (4) is trivial.

  \emph{Proof that (4) implies (2).}
  The idea is to glue trees of increasing height into an infinite tree in the ultrapower, and to observe that an infinite tree has $2^{\aleph_0}$ separated leaves, which no separable dual can accommodate.
  Let $\mathcal{U}$ be as in~(4), and suppose that for some $\delta$ there are $\delta$-trees $(\rho^{(n)}_\eta,\sigma^{(n)}_s,\gamma_n,\theta_n)$ of every height $n$.
  Pass to a set in $\mathcal{U}$ on which $\theta_n=\theta$ is constant, and let $\gamma=\lim_{n,\mathcal{U}}\gamma_n$.
  For an infinite branch $\eta\in2^\mathbb{N}$, put $x_\eta=(\rho^{(n)}_{\eta|n})_n$, with $\eta|n$ the initial segment of length $n$, and for $s\in2^{<\mathbb{N}}$, put $y_s=(\sigma^{(n)}_s)_n$, with arbitrary entries for $n\le|s|$.
  If $s{}^\frown \iota\sqsubseteq\eta$, then we have $s{}^\frown \iota\sqsubseteq\eta|n$ for all $n>|s|$, and passing to the limit, we have $\theta(\Phi^\mathcal{U}_C(x_\eta,y_s)-\gamma)\ge\delta/2$ if $\iota=1$ and $\le-\delta/2$ if $\iota=0$.
  This is an infinite $\delta$-tree for $\Phi^\mathcal{U}_C$, which proves the statement of \cref{thm:uniform} on infinite $\delta$-trees.

  Now suppose that $\Phi^\mathcal{U}_C$ is stable.
  After an affine rescaling to values in $[0,1]$, which multiplies gaps by
  $c=1/(2\|C\|)$, Iovino’s theorem~\cite[Theorem~3.3]{Iovino:1999c} gives a reflexive Banach space
  $E$ and maps $u\colon\mathfrak{D}(H_1)^\mathbb{N}\to E$ and $v\colon\mathfrak{D}(H_2)^\mathbb{N}\to E^*$, with values in the unit balls, such that $c(\Phi^\mathcal{U}_C+\|C\|)=\langle u(\cdot),v(\cdot)\rangle$.
  Let $Y$ be the closed span in $E^*$ of the countably many vectors $v(y_s)$.
  The space $Y$ is separable and reflexive, so its dual $Y^*$ is separable.
  If $\eta\ne\eta'$ first differ after the segment $s$, then
  $|\langle u(x_\eta)-u(x_{\eta'}),v(y_s)\rangle|\ge c\delta$, so the restrictions of the vectors $u(x_\eta)$ to $Y$ are $2^{\aleph_0}$ points of $Y^*$ at mutual distance at least $c\delta$, which is impossible in a separable space.
  Hence the function $\Phi^\mathcal{U}_C$ is unstable, contradicting~(4).

  Finally, an unstable observable has infinite ladders by \cref{prop:inst-ladder}, so it is not uniformly stable.

title: Example
body_md:
\label{exa:sector}
  Let both $H_1$ and $H_2$ be the Hilbert space $\bigoplus_{n\ge1}\mathbb{C}^n$, with orthonormal bases $(e^n_i)_{i\le n}$ of the summands;
  for instance, the summand $\mathbb{C}^{2j+1}$ is the spin-$j$ representation, with basis $|j,m\rangle$ ordered by $m$.
  Put
  \[
    C_{\mathrm{sec}}=\sum_{n\ge1}\ \sum_{1\le i\le l\le n}|e^n_i\rangle\langle e^n_i|\otimes|e^n_l\rangle\langle e^n_l| ,
  \]
  the projection onto “both systems lie in the same sector, and Alice’s level does not exceed Bob’s”.
  In the sector $\mathbb{C}^n$, the states $e^n_1,\dots,e^n_n$ form a $1$-ladder of length $n$, so the projection $C_{\mathrm{sec}}$ is not uniformly stable and has $1$-trees of every finite height.
  The projection $C_{\mathrm{sec}}$ is, however, stable:
  the effective observable $T_{C_{\mathrm{sec}}}(\rho)$ depends only on the diagonal entries $\rho^n_{ii}$, and $T_{C_{\mathrm{sec}}}=J\circ a$ with
  \[
    a\colon\mathcal{T}(H_1)\to\Bigl(\bigoplus_n\ell^1_n\Bigr)_{\ell^2},\quad
    a(\rho)=\bigl((\rho^n_{ii})_{i\le n}\bigr)_n,
    \qquad
    J\bigl((w_n)_n\bigr)=\bigoplus_n\sum_{l\le n}\Bigl(\sum_{i\le l}w_{n,i}\Bigr)|e^n_l\rangle\langle e^n_l| .
  \]
  Here $\|a(\rho)\|\le\sum_n\sum_i|\rho^n_{ii}|\le\|\rho\|_1$ and $\|J\|\le1$, and the $\ell^2$-sum of finite-dimensional spaces is reflexive, so \cref{thm:weakcompact}(4) applies.

name: Stable but not uniformly stable

label: thm:growth
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:growth}
  Let $C\in B(H_1\otimes H_2)$ be self-adjoint, and let $\delta>0$ be given.
  \begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\arabic*)}]
  \par\hangindent 40\p@
    If $d=d_C(\delta)$ is finite, then for all $n$ we have
    \[
      \operatorname{gr}_C(n,\delta)\le\binom{n}{\le d}\le\Bigl(\frac{\mathrm{e} n}{d}\Bigr)^{d}\qquad(n\ge d\ge1),
    \]
    which is a polynomial in $n$ of degree $d$.
  \par\hangindent 40\p@
    If $d_C(\delta)$ is infinite, then we have $\operatorname{gr}_C(n,\delta)=2^n$ for every $n$.
  \end{enumerate}
  Consequently, the observable $C$ is uniformly stable if and only if $\operatorname{gr}_C(\cdot,\delta)$ grows polynomially for every $\delta>0$;
  otherwise it equals $2^n$ for some $\delta$.
  In particular, unstable observables have exponential growth.
head: environment
name: Polynomial versus exponential growth

title: Proof
body_md:
Statement~(2) holds because a $\delta$-tree of height at least $n$, restricted to its nodes of length less than $n$ and one leaf above each branch of length $n$, realizes every branch of a probe tree of depth $n$.
  For~(1), the idea is that at each probe, at most one of the two halves of the remaining preparations can carry a tree as tall as the whole set.
  Fix $\gamma$, $\theta$ and a probe tree of depth $n$.
  We show by induction on $n$ that the number of branches realized by elements of a set $\mathcal{R}\subseteq\mathfrak{D}(H_1)$ is at most $\binom{n}{\le d(\mathcal{R})}$, with the convention that $\binom{n}{\le-1}=0$.
  For $n=0$ this is clear.
  For $n\ge1$, let $\mathcal{R}_\iota$ be the set of elements of $\mathcal{R}$ that satisfy the inequality for $\iota$ at the root.
  The sets $\mathcal{R}_0$ and $\mathcal{R}_1$ are disjoint, because the two inequalities are separated by $\delta$.
  A branch $\iota{}^\frown \eta'$ is realized in $\mathcal{R}$ exactly when $\eta'$ is realized in $\mathcal{R}_\iota$ for the subtree $(\sigma_{\iota{}^\frown s})_s$ of depth $n-1$.
  We have $d(\mathcal{R}_\iota)\le d(\mathcal{R})$, and the two numbers $d(\mathcal{R}_0)$ and $d(\mathcal{R}_1)$ cannot both equal $d(\mathcal{R})$:
  two $\delta$-trees of height $d(\mathcal{R})$ with leaves in $\mathcal{R}_0$ and in $\mathcal{R}_1$, placed above the root probe $\sigma_\emptyset$, would form a $\delta$-tree of height $d(\mathcal{R})+1$ with leaves in $\mathcal{R}$.
  By induction and Pascal’s rule, the number of realized branches is at most $\binom{n-1}{\le d}+\binom{n-1}{\le d-1}=\binom{n}{\le d}$, with $d=d(\mathcal{R})$.
  The bound $\binom{n}{\le d}\le(\mathrm{e} n/d)^d$ is standard.
  The last statements follow from \cref{thm:trees,thm:uniform}.

label: rem:rowbottom
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:rowbottom}
  Stability has many equivalent characterizations, but its original definition was a growth condition.
  Rowbottom~\cite{Rowbottom:1964} called a complete theory
  $T$ \emph{stable in} an infinite cardinal $\lambda$ if for every model $\mathcal{M}$ of $T$ and every set $A\subseteq\mathcal{M}$ of cardinality $\lambda$, the space $S_1(A)$ of complete $1$-types over $A$ has cardinality at most $\lambda$.
  The reverse inequality is trivial, since distinct elements of $A$ realize distinct types over $A$;
  so stability in $\lambda$ says that $|S_1(A)|=|A|$, that is, the number of types grows linearly with the number of parameters, whereas a priori it can be as large as $2^\lambda$.
  For a single formula $\varphi$, stability is equivalent to the bound $|S_\varphi(A)|\le|A|$ for every infinite set $A$ of parameters (see \cite[Chapter~1]{Pillay:1996} and~\cite{Shelah:1990a}).
  \cref{thm:growth} is a finite and adaptive counterpart of this condition:
  the number of preparations resolved by $n$ probes is bounded by a polynomial in $n$.
  For an infinite cardinal $\lambda$ and an integer $d\ge1$, we have $\lambda^d=\lambda$, so on infinite parameter sets the distinction between linear and polynomial bounds disappears.

label: thm:perceptron
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:perceptron}
  Let $C\in B(H_1\otimes H_2)$ be self-adjoint, and suppose that $\varphi_C(\rho,\sigma)=\langle u(\rho),v(\sigma)\rangle$ for maps $u$ and $v$ into a Hilbert space $\mathcal{H}$ with $\|u(\rho)\|\le R_u$ and $\|v(\sigma)\|\le R_v$.
  Then for every $\delta>0$, we have
  \[
    d_C(\delta)\le16\Bigl(\frac{R_uR_v}{\delta}\Bigr)^{2},
  \]
  independently of the dimensions of $H_1$ and $H_2$.
  In particular, we have $d_C(\delta)\le16/\delta^2$ for the swap operator $F$ and for $[A=B]$, and $d_C(\delta)\le4/\delta^2$ for the swap test $P_+$ and the Hong--Ou--Mandel projection $P_-$.
head: environment
name: Linear bound for Hilbert-factorable observables

title: Proof
body_md:
The idea is to run the perceptron along the tree, always moving to the child that contradicts its prediction;
  the leaf reached at the end is a linear separator with margin $\delta/2$, and the perceptron makes few mistakes against such a separator.
  Regard the Hilbert space as a real inner product space with $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{\mathbb{R}}=\operatorname{Re}\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle$;
  since $\varphi_C$ is real, we have $\varphi_C=\langle u,v\rangle_{\mathbb{R}}$.
  Let a $\delta$-tree of height $n$ be given, with threshold $\gamma$ and sign $\theta$.
  The tree requires values of $\varphi_C$ on both sides of $\gamma$, so we have $|\gamma|\le R_uR_v$.
  Put $\hat{u}(\rho)=(u(\rho),R_u)$ and $\hat{v}(\sigma)=(v(\sigma),-\gamma/R_u)$ in $\mathcal{H}\oplus\mathbb{R}$;
  then $\langle\hat{u}(\rho),\hat{v}(\sigma)\rangle_{\mathbb{R}}=\varphi_C(\rho,\sigma)-\gamma$, $\|\hat{u}\|\le\sqrt2R_u$ and $\|\hat{v}\|\le\sqrt2R_v$.
  Start with $z_0=0$ at the root.
  At the node $s$ reached at step $i$, let $\hat{y}=\operatorname{sign}\langle z_i,\hat{v}(\sigma_s)\rangle_{\mathbb{R}}$, with
  $\operatorname{sign}0=1$, move to the child whose label $y=\theta(2\iota-1)$ equals $-\hat{y}$, and put $z_{i+1}=z_i+y\,\hat{v}(\sigma_s)$.
  After $n$ steps we reach a branch $\eta$, and its leaf $\hat{u}^*=\hat{u}(\rho_\eta)$ satisfies $y\langle\hat{u}^*,\hat{v}(\sigma_s)\rangle_{\mathbb{R}}\ge\delta/2$ at every step.
  Hence we have $\langle\hat{u}^*,z_n\rangle_{\mathbb{R}}\ge n\delta/2$, while $\|z_n\|^2\le\sum_i\|\hat{v}(\sigma_{s_i})\|^2\le2nR_v^2$, because each step adds $2y\langle z_i,\hat{v}(\sigma_{s_i})\rangle_{\mathbb{R}}\le0$ to the cross term.
  By the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality, we have $n\delta/2\le\sqrt2R_u\cdot\sqrt{2n}\,R_v$, that is, $n\le16(R_uR_v/\delta)^2$.

  For $F$ and $[A=B]$, we have $R_u,R_v\le1$ (see \cref{sec:swap} and \cref{prop:comparison}).
  Since $\varphi_{P_\pm}=\frac12(1\pm\varphi_F)$, every $\delta$-tree for $P_\pm$ is a $2\delta$-tree for $F$.

label: rem:sfat
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:sfat}
  The proof of \cref{thm:perceptron} uses the threshold only through the probe vectors $\hat{v}(\sigma_s)$, and the bound $|\gamma|\le R_uR_v$ holds at each node separately, since every node has leaves on both sides of its threshold.
  The proof therefore applies without change to trees in which the threshold $\gamma_s$ depends on the node $s$.
  Consequently, the response class $\{\sigma\mapsto\varphi_C(\rho,\sigma):\rho\in\mathfrak{D}(H_1)\}$
  of a Hilbert-factorable observable has sequential fat-shattering dimension at most
  $16(R_uR_v/\delta)^2$ at scale $\delta$ in the sense of~\cite{Rakhlin-Sridharan-Tewari:2015}, and so it is online learnable in that sense, with bounds independent of the dimension.

label: prop:littlestone
title: Proposition
head: environment
name: Mistake bound equals tree dimension

title: Proof
body_md:
If there is a tree of height $n$, an adversary walks down it, choosing at each node the child that contradicts the learner’s prediction;
  the leaf reached is a preparation consistent with all answers, so every learner makes $n$ mistakes.
  Conversely, run Littlestone’s standard optimal algorithm:
  keep the set $V$ of preparations consistent with the answers so far;
  for a probe $\sigma$, let $V^1$ and $V^0$ be the sets of elements of $V$ above $\gamma+\delta/2$ and below $\gamma-\delta/2$, and predict the side $\iota$ for which $d(V^\iota)$ is larger, in the notation of \cref{sec:growth}.
  Arguing as in the proof of \cref{thm:growth}, the numbers $d(V^0)$ and $d(V^1)$ cannot both equal $d(V)$, so after a mistake the new consistent set $V^{1-\iota}$ satisfies $d(V^{1-\iota})<d(V)$.
  Since the true preparation stays in $V$, we have $d(V)\ge0$ throughout, and there are at most $d_\gamma$ mistakes.
  The second statement follows from \cref{thm:uniform}.

label: prop:operatorsystem
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:operatorsystem}
  The set $\mathcal{O}$ of stable observables is a norm-closed operator system:
  a self-adjoint linear subspace of $B(H_1\otimes H_2)$ that contains $I$ and is closed in the norm topology.
  The set $\mathcal{O}$ contains the minimal tensor product $B(H_1)\otimes_{\min}B(H_2)$ and every observable whose expectation factors through a Hilbert space.
  The same holds for the set of uniformly stable observables.

title: Proof
body_md:
The identity $I=I\otimes I$ is stable, and for density operators we have $\varphi_{C^*}=\overline{\varphi_C}$.
  Linear combinations and norm limits are handled by \cref{lem:preservation}(a) and~(b), and for uniform stability the same lemma applies to $\Phi^\mathcal{U}_C$.
  The last two statements are \cref{thm:stable}, \cref{prop:hilbertfactor} and \cref{prop:uniform-examples}.

label: cor:orthoposet
title: Corollary
head: environment
name: Orthocomplements and orthogonal sums

title: Proof
body_md:
If the projections $P$ and $Q$ are stable, then the projections $I-P$, $P+Q$ (when $PQ=0$) and $Q-P$ (when $P\le Q$) are linear combinations of stable observables, and hence they are stable by \cref{prop:operatorsystem}.
  Thus the stable projections are closed under orthocomplements and orthogonal sums, and the orthomodular law, which holds for all projections on $H_1\otimes H_2$, holds among them.

label: prop:meet
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:meet}
  If $H_1$ and $H_2$ are infinite-dimensional, then there are projections $P_1$ and $P_2$ in $B(H_1)\otimes_{\min}B(H_2)$, hence uniformly stable, whose meet $P_1\wedge P_2$ is unstable.
head: environment
name: The boundary: meets

title: Proof
body_md:
The idea is to hide the order projection inside the intersection of two subspaces that are compact perturbations of a product projection, by tilting each matrix entry into a fresh direction through a small angle, in opposite senses for the two subspaces.
  Let $(e_k)\cup(e'_k)$ be an orthonormal sequence in $H_1$ and $(f_l)\cup(f'_l)$ one in $H_2$, and let $P_{k<l}$ be the order projection built from $(e_k)$ and $(f_l)$.
  For $k\ge l$, let $\zeta_k=1/k$ and
  \[
    n_{kl}=\cos\zeta_k\,e_k\otimes f_l+\sin\zeta_k\,e'_k\otimes f'_l,\qquad
    n'_{kl}=\cos\zeta_k\,e_k\otimes f_l-\sin\zeta_k\,e'_k\otimes f'_l,
  \]
  and let $P_1$ and $P_2$ be the projections onto the closed subspaces $\operatorname{ran}P_{k<l}\oplus\overline{\operatorname{span}}\{n_{kl}:k\ge l\}$ and $\operatorname{ran}P_{k<l}\oplus\overline{\operatorname{span}}\{n'_{kl}:k\ge l\}$.
  The planes spanned by $e_k\otimes f_l$ and $e'_k\otimes f'_l$ are mutually orthogonal and orthogonal to the range of $P_{k<l}$, and in each of them the lines through $n_{kl}$ and $n'_{kl}$ meet only in $0$, since $0<\zeta_k<\pi/2$.
  Both subspaces are block diagonal for this decomposition, so their intersection is the range of $P_{k<l}$, that is, $P_1\wedge P_2=P_{k<l}$, which is unstable by \cref{thm:unstable}.

  Let $Q_1$ and $Q_2$ be the projections onto the closed spans of $(e_k)$ and $(f_l)$.
  The operator $P_1-Q_1\otimes Q_2$ is the orthogonal sum over $k\ge l$ of the rank-two operators $|n_{kl}\rangle\langle n_{kl}|-|e_k\otimes f_l\rangle\langle e_k\otimes f_l|$, of norm $\sin\zeta_k$.
  For every $\varepsilon>0$, only finitely many pairs $k\ge l$ have $1/k\ge\varepsilon$, so this sum is compact.
  Since $Q_1\otimes Q_2$ and the compact operators lie in $B(H_1)\otimes_{\min}B(H_2)$, so does $P_1$, and likewise $P_2$.
  Conclude with \cref{thm:stable} and \cref{prop:uniform-examples}.
